content: Mucopolysaccharidoses (MPS) are a group of lysosomal storage disorders (LSDs) characterized by the accumulation of glycosaminoglycans (GAGs), which are extracellular macromolecules. These macromolecules play a critical role in the structural integrity of connective tissue and cartilage. Additionally, they are involved in regulating various biochemical processes, including coagulation, immune responses, pathogen recognition and clearance via the complement system, intercellular communication, and wound healing. Due to their complex structure, the complete lysosomal degradation of GAGs requires multiple enzymes. A deficiency in any of these enzymes results in the accumulation of GAGs, particularly within chondrocytes and the extracellular matrix, leading to inflammation and programmed cell death (apoptosis). Morquio syndrome, also known as MPS type IV, is one of the seven recognized phenotypes of MPS. It is further divided into two subtypes based on the specific enzymatic deficiency. Type IV A is caused by a deficiency in galactosamine-6-sulfatase (GALNS), while type IV B results from a deficiency in beta-galactosidase. Both deficiencies impair the breakdown of keratan sulfate (KS), leading to its accumulation in various tissues, including the skeletal system, visceral organs, heart valves, and eyes. This review focuses on MPS IV A. The clinical manifestations of MPS IV A include skeletal dysplasia, which presents as short stature, pectus carinatum, kyphosis, joint abnormalities, and odontoid hypoplasia. Other features include hepatomegaly (enlarged liver), dental anomalies, corneal clouding, hearing impairments, and heart valve defects. Enzyme replacement therapy (ERT) involves the intravenous administration of recombinant enzymes and was initially developed as a treatment for Gaucher disease. It has since become an established therapeutic approach for several LSDs, including MPS IV A. In 2014, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration approved a recombinant human GALNS enzyme (rhGALNS), marketed as elosulfase alfa (Vimizim®), for the treatment of MPS IV A. ERT for MPS IV A is generally considered safe, with hypersensitivity reactions being uncommon and anaphylaxis being rare. Reported adverse effects include vomiting, fever, and headaches. In MPS IV A, as in other LSDs such as Gaucher disease, the deficiency or malfunction of a specific enzyme leads to the accumulation of its substrate—in this case, keratan sulfate. ERT involves the systemic administration of a synthetically produced enzyme, which is taken up by cells through mannose-6-phosphate receptors on the plasma membrane. This mechanism allows the enzyme to enter the lysosomal compartment and perform its function. The evidence supporting the efficacy of ERT in MPS IV A is limited, as is often the case with ultra-rare orphan disorders. This is due to the small number of affected individuals, the heterogeneity of the disease, its chronic nature with diverse clinical manifestations, and variations in study protocols. These factors make it challenging to conduct randomized controlled trials (RCTs). Additionally, the global distribution of patients necessitates multiple clinical trial sites, each with a small number of participants, further complicating research efforts. Consequently, much of the available evidence comes from non-randomized studies, such as patient registries. For instance, a PubMed search using the terms MPS IV A and randomized controlled trial yields only six results, whereas combining MPS IV A with cohort studies produces 40 studies. Given these challenges, producing a robust evidence-based systematic review on the efficacy of ERT for MPS IV A using traditional Cochrane methodology is fraught with limitations. This issue has been previously highlighted in a Cochrane Review on Gaucher disease. To address these challenges, the authors propose conducting a Cochrane Review that incorporates data from both RCTs and non-randomized studies to evaluate the efficacy of ERT for MPS IV A. This approach aims to determine whether such a methodology can enhance the systematic review process for ultra-rare disorders.
